Batteries

How a home solar battery actually works

Chemistry, inverters, usable capacity and the difference between power and energy — explained without the sales language.

Published 12 August 2026Updated 15 October 20268 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

A home battery does one simple job: it moves electricity from the time it was generated to the time you want to use it. Everything else — the chemistry, the inverter, the app — exists to make that move safe, efficient and measurable.

The five parts of the system

  • Battery modules: the cells that store energy, usually lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) for stationary home storage, or nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) in some products.
  • Battery management system (BMS): monitors cell voltage, temperature and current, and protects the pack from conditions that shorten its life.
  • Inverter or hybrid inverter: converts direct current (DC) from the panels and battery into alternating current (AC) for your home, and back again for storage.
  • Metering and monitoring: measures what is generated, imported, exported and stored — the data that makes optimisation possible.
  • Protection and isolation: circuit protection, isolation points and ventilation or clearance arrangements required by the relevant Australian installation standards.

Standards and installation matter as much as the product

Battery installation in Australia is governed by installation standards and state electrical safety requirements that set out clearances, ventilation, signage, protection and documentation. The current edition of the applicable standards and your installer's accreditation are the authority here — not a product brochure.

Energy versus power — the two numbers that get confused

Capacity is measured in kilowatt hours (kWh) and describes how much energy the battery can store. Power output is measured in kilowatts (kW) and describes how much can flow at any instant. A battery with plenty of kWh but modest kW may be unable to start a large load, while a high-power battery with small capacity will empty quickly.

Two further figures change the usefulness of the headline number. Usable capacity is what remains after the depth-of-discharge limit, which many manufacturers set between 90% and 100% for LiFePO4 products but which can be lower. Round-trip efficiency is how much energy you get back out compared with what you put in — typically in the order of 85% to 95% for modern systems once conversion losses are counted.

Example: a battery with 10 kWh of nameplate capacity
FigureIllustrative valueWhat it means for you
Nameplate capacity10 kWhThe marketing number on the specification sheet
Usable capacity at 90% DoD9 kWhWhat you can actually draw before the BMS limits output
Round-trip efficiency at 90%8.1 kWhEnergy delivered to the house after losses

That example is an illustration of the maths, not a product claim. Every product has its own datasheet — the point is to compare products on usable energy delivered, not on the largest number in the brochure.

AC-coupled or DC-coupled?

A DC-coupled battery connects to a hybrid inverter, sharing the conversion equipment with the solar array. This is common on new installations and can be slightly more efficient because there are fewer conversions.

An AC-coupled battery has its own inverter and sits alongside whatever solar inverter you already own. It is the usual choice when retrofitting storage to an existing system, particularly where the original inverter is in good condition but is not hybrid-capable.

What backup power really involves

During a blackout, a grid-connected solar system must shut down unless it has specific anti-islanding protection and backup capability. This is a safety requirement: the network must not be energised by your system while crews are working on it.

A battery with backup capability can supply a dedicated backup circuit — or, with suitable equipment and capacity, the whole house. What you can run depends on continuous and peak power ratings and on which circuits were wired into the backup path. If outage protection matters, decide that before installation, because it changes the wiring design.

What shortens a battery's life

  • Frequent deep cycling, especially in hot conditions.
  • High ambient temperatures — placement in a hot garage or in direct western sun is a design decision, not a detail.
  • Extended time spent at very high or very low state of charge.
  • Poor ventilation or crowded mounting that traps heat.

This is why reputable manufacturers publish warranted throughput limits and cycle counts, and why placement and ventilation are part of the design conversation rather than the installation morning.

How to judge whether storage is worth it for you

  1. Look at how much energy you export and what you are paid for it.
  2. Look at how much you import in the evening and overnight, and what you pay for it.
  3. Estimate what share of that evening import a battery of a given size could realistically cover.
  4. Compare the installed cost after any incentives against that annual value.

Our savings estimator does exactly this arithmetic and shows every assumption it uses, so you can see which input changes the outcome most for your household.

Key takeaways

  • Capacity (kWh) is how much energy a battery stores; power (kW) is how quickly it can deliver it. Both decide what jobs it can do.
  • Usable capacity and round-trip efficiency mean delivered energy is always less than the nameplate figure.
  • DC-coupled suits new builds; AC-coupled suits most retrofits onto existing solar.
  • Backup power depends on wiring and peak ratings, and is planned before installation — not after.
  • Heat, deep cycling and placement influence lifespan as much as the brand on the box.
